topics.title: Wildlife of the African Savanna
passage: Africa's savannas are wide, grassy plains dotted with scattered trees, and they are home to some of the most famous animals on Earth. Elephants, lions, giraffes, and zebras all share this open landscape, along with millions of wildebeest that gather in massive herds. The mix of grass, occasional rain, and warm weather year-round makes the savanna an ideal home for large plant-eating animals, which in turn attract the predators that hunt them.

Every year, more than a million wildebeest travel across the Serengeti in East Africa in search of fresh grass and water, joined by zebras and gazelles along the way. This journey, called the Great Migration, follows the pattern of the wet and dry seasons. Traveling in such enormous herds offers the animals some protection, since predators like lions and hyenas find it harder to target one individual within a huge, moving crowd.

Lions are the savanna's top predator and live in family groups called prides, usually made up of related females, their cubs, and a smaller number of males. Female lions do most of the hunting, often working together to surround and catch prey such as zebras or antelope. Because hunting is difficult and does not always succeed, lions may rest for up to twenty hours a day to conserve energy between hunts.

Giraffes, the tallest land animals on Earth, have long necks that let them reach leaves high in acacia trees that other animals cannot get to, reducing competition for food. Their height also helps them spot approaching predators from a distance across the flat grassland. Despite their size, giraffes can run in short bursts and deliver a powerful kick, which is usually enough to keep even a hungry lion away.

Human activity has changed much of the savanna landscape through farming, cities, and roads, which has reduced the space available for wild animals to migrate and find food. Many African countries have created large national parks and reserves, such as the Serengeti and the Maasai Mara, specifically to protect these ecosystems. Conservation programs work to balance the needs of local communities with the survival of savanna wildlife for future generations.

topics.title: The Amazon Rainforest: Life in South America
passage: The Amazon Rainforest stretches across much of South America, covering parts of Brazil, Peru, Colombia, and several other countries. It is the largest rainforest on Earth and contains an incredible variety of life, from tiny insects to massive jaguars. Scientists believe the Amazon may be home to roughly ten percent of all known species on the planet, even though it covers only a small fraction of Earth's land surface.

One reason the Amazon supports so much life is its layered structure. The tallest trees form an upper layer called the emergent layer, below which sits a thick canopy of overlapping treetops that blocks most sunlight from reaching the ground. Beneath the canopy is a darker understory, and finally the forest floor, where fallen leaves decompose quickly in the warm, humid air. Each layer provides a different habitat, so many species can live in the same area without directly competing for space.

The jaguar is the largest cat in the Americas and a top predator of the Amazon. Unlike many big cats, jaguars are strong swimmers and often hunt near rivers, catching fish, turtles, and even caimans, a relative of the alligator. Their powerful jaws can bite through the tough shells of turtles and the skulls of prey, a bite force stronger than that of lions or tigers relative to body size.

The Amazon River, which flows through the rainforest, is home to the pink river dolphin, one of the few freshwater dolphin species in the world. These dolphins use sound, called echolocation, to navigate the muddy river water, where visibility is often very poor. Poison dart frogs, some of the most colorful animals in the rainforest, also make their home here; their bright colors warn predators that their skin contains toxins, a defense strategy called warning coloration.

Despite its size, the Amazon faces serious threats from deforestation, as trees are cleared for farming, cattle ranching, and logging. Losing large areas of rainforest does not just affect the plants and animals that live there; scientists say the Amazon also plays an important role in producing oxygen and absorbing carbon dioxide for the entire planet. International organizations and local governments continue to work on ways to slow deforestation and protect this unique ecosystem.

topics.title: Australia's Unusual Marsupials
passage: Australia is home to a group of animals called marsupials, which are mammals that carry and nurse their young in a pouch. Kangaroos, koalas, wombats, and Tasmanian devils are all marsupials, and many of them exist nowhere else on Earth. Because Australia has been separated from other continents by ocean for millions of years, its animals evolved in isolation, developing traits found in few other places in the world.

Kangaroos are perhaps Australia's most recognizable animal, known for hopping on their powerful hind legs instead of walking on all four. A newborn kangaroo, called a joey, is tiny and undeveloped at birth, sometimes no bigger than a jellybean, and must crawl into its mother's pouch to continue growing and nursing for several months. Kangaroos can hop at speeds over thirty-five miles per hour and use their large tails for balance.

Koalas spend most of their lives in eucalyptus trees, eating almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves, which are tough, low in nutrients, and mildly toxic to most other animals. To handle this difficult diet, koalas sleep up to twenty hours a day to conserve energy, since eucalyptus provides very little fuel for activity. Their strong sense of smell also helps them choose the least toxic leaves from a tree before eating.

The Tasmanian devil, found mainly on the island of Tasmania, is the largest surviving carnivorous marsupial in the world. Despite its name, it is roughly the size of a small dog, but it has an extremely powerful bite for its size and a loud, startling screech used to warn off rivals during feeding. Tasmanian devils mostly scavenge dead animals rather than hunting live prey, playing an important role in cleaning up the ecosystem.

Many of Australia's marsupials face serious threats today, including habitat loss from land development and diseases such as a contagious facial tumor disease that has sharply reduced Tasmanian devil populations. Wildlife groups have set up breeding programs and protected reserves to help vulnerable species recover. Because these animals are found almost nowhere else, their survival depends heavily on continued conservation efforts within Australia itself.

topics.title: Survivors of the Arctic and Antarctic
passage: The Arctic, at the top of the world, and Antarctica, at the bottom, are two of the coldest and harshest places on Earth, yet both are home to animals specially adapted to survive extreme cold. Although people sometimes picture polar bears and penguins living together, this is a common mistake: polar bears live only in the Arctic, while penguins live mostly in Antarctica and the Southern Hemisphere, and the two species never naturally meet in the wild.

Polar bears are the largest land predators in the Arctic, built for a life spent mostly hunting on sea ice. A thick layer of fat called blubber, combined with dense fur, keeps them warm in temperatures far below freezing. Polar bears primarily hunt seals, waiting patiently near breathing holes in the ice for a seal to surface, sometimes waiting motionless for hours at a time before striking.

In Antarctica, emperor penguins face some of the harshest breeding conditions of any bird on Earth. During the brutal Antarctic winter, male emperor penguins balance a single egg on their feet for about two months, keeping it warm under a fold of skin while enduring freezing winds and going without food the entire time. Meanwhile, females travel to the ocean to feed, returning just as the chicks are ready to hatch.

Both polar regions support surprising amounts of ocean life beneath the ice. Arctic waters are home to narwhals, sometimes called the "unicorns of the sea" because of the long, spiraled tusk males grow from a tooth. In the Southern Ocean around Antarctica, krill, small shrimp-like creatures, exist in massive numbers and form the base of the food chain, feeding everything from fish to penguins to enormous blue whales.

Climate change poses a major threat to both polar regions, as rising temperatures cause sea ice to melt earlier in the year and form later, shrinking the hunting grounds polar bears depend on and changing the ocean conditions krill need to thrive. Scientists closely monitor these changes because a shrinking food supply at the base of the food chain, like krill, can eventually affect nearly every other species living in the region.
